title: Right intention
hookLine: intentions of letting go, of goodwill, of harmlessness (MN 117)

cards: Two people hand you a cup of coffee. Same cup, same coffee, same smile. One cares whether your morning goes well.
The other wants something from you this afternoon. From the outside, there's no difference at all. From the inside, they're walking two different roads.
That inside part, the aim behind the act, is the second spoke of the wheel. After right view comes the question: now that you see, what are you aiming at?

teach.h: SANKAPPA: WHAT THE MIND IS SET ON.
teach.b: The Pali is samma sankappa. Sankappa means thought, intention, resolve: what the mind is set on. Rhys Davids, translating the first sermon, called it right aspirations.
The suttas, in the Great Forty and in the sutta that lists all eight factors, define it in three parts: the intention of letting go, of goodwill, and of harmlessness.

Letting go, nekkhamma, is the aim of wanting less, of not being run by craving. Goodwill is wishing others well instead of ill. Harmlessness is the aim of not causing pain, which teachers link with compassion.
Each aim is the medicine for a poison: letting go for greed, goodwill for ill will, harmlessness for cruelty. Notice where right intention sits.

teach.h: PART OF THE TRAINING IN WISDOM.
teach.b: With right view, it makes up the training in wisdom. Isn't intention about will, not wisdom?
But in the way the path is taught, seeing clearly and aiming well belong together: someone who sees that craving brings dukkha begins to aim away from it. And look at the order of the list.
Speech, action and livelihood come after intention.

teach.h: THE AIM COMES BEFORE THE ACT.
teach.b: The aim is set before the mouth opens or the hand moves.
Right intention isn't a promise to be perfect. It's choosing the aim behind the cup of coffee.

how: Buddhist teachers commonly present right intention through its three parts, renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness, and students may set an intention at the start of a day, a meditation or a retreat.

o: right intention: aiming at goodwill and no harm
a firm plan for reaching your goals

games.q: match each intention to the poison it treats.
p: intention, what the mind is set on

s: right intention belongs to the training in meditation
with right view, it makes up the training in wisdom.
right intention has three parts: letting go, goodwill, harmlessness
that's how the suttas define it.
right intention means vowing to be perfect
it's choosing a direction for the mind, not a promise of perfection.

games.q: two people hand you identical cups of coffee. one cares about your morning; one wants a favor later. by today's teaching, where's the difference?
o: in the intention behind the act.
games.why: the act looks the same; right intention is about the aim behind it, which shapes everything that follows.

practice: Choose one of the three aims, letting go, goodwill or harmlessness, and let it become a short phrase in your own words: today, I'll want a little less; or, today, I'll wish people well; or, today, I won't add to anyone's pain.
Breathe it in and out a few times, not as a vow, just pointing the compass.

wordCard.voice: Samma sankappa. Right intention: aiming at letting go, at goodwill, and at harmlessness. The second factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali sammā saṅkappa: right intention or right resolve, the second factor of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: intend it. The aim is set before the hand moves. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: MN 117 (Mahacattarisaka Sutta) and SN 45.8 (Vibhanga Sutta), right intention defined
